h1: Hardy–Weinberg from the Recessive Allele Frequency
summary:
If you already know q, the recessive allele's frequency, the rest follows directly: p is 1 − q, and the genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². It returns dominant allele frequency (p), AA frequency, aa frequency (carriers) and aa frequency (affected), and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator spells out the three genotypes, the carrier rate and the ratio of carriers to affected individuals. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hardy–Weinberg from the Recessive Allele Frequency
sections.html:
p = 1 − q; AA = p²; Aa = 2pq; aa = q²

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
qrecessive allele frequency0–1
pdominant allele frequency0–1
2pqheterozygote frequency0–1

sections.title: How do I use the Hardy–Weinberg from the Recessive Allele Frequency?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: recessive allele frequency (q) of 0.2.

Substituting them into the formula gives dominant allele frequency (p) of 0.8, aa frequency of 0.64, aa frequency (carriers) of 0.32, aa frequency (affected) of 0.04, carriers per affected individual of 8 :1, affected share of the population of 4%.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The ratio of carriers to affected people is 2p/q, which shows how sharply carriers outnumber patients as q falls.

  • These are expected frequencies for a large randomly mating population, not counts for a particular family.

  • For a sex-linked trait the arithmetic differs: males carry one X, so their frequency of the recessive phenotype equals q rather than q².

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Using q² for an X-linked recessive trait in males.
  • Rounding p and q so that they no longer sum to exactly 1 before squaring.

faq.q: Is the carrier frequency 2pq or q?
faq.a: 2pq — the heterozygote frequency. q alone is the allele frequency.
Then p is 0.5 too and the three genotype frequencies are 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25.

faq.q: What does the Hardy–Weinberg from the Recessive Allele Frequency actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns dominant allele frequency (p), AA frequency, aa frequency (carriers) and aa frequency (affected). Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
